# Don versus the internet

*Court is in session. In the matter of Don, the register hears the evidence — the attestation, the marks, and the forms that stand accused.*

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Don
- **Original script:** —
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Convention:** the tradition’s own scholarly transliteration standard
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 140 of 597

## The Charge

That the name **Don** is routinely written in forms that move, drop, or invent its marks — and that each such form teaches the reader a different, lesser name. The register's task is to separate the honest fallback from the outright false.

## The Defense of the Canonical Form

The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Don** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form the tradition’s convention demands.

## The Character Witness

The plain form *don* differs from the canonical **Don** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## Mitigating Circumstances

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — the tradition’s standard — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Don**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Don** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

## The Verdict

So the register finds: **Don**, canonical; *don*, equally canonical; the contested forms, recorded with their support; the false forms, ruled against with their violations named. Every line of that finding cites its evidence, and the evidence is open to any reader — the register asks to be checked, not trusted. The temple keeps the canonical form at [/don/](/don/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 10 cited sources — The Mabinogi, Fourth Branch (Math fab Mathonwy) — trans. Sioned Davies (Oxford, 2007); Welsh text ed. Ifor Williams, Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930), Culhwch ac Olwen, ed. Rachel Bromwich and D. Simon Evans (Cardiff, 1992) — Amaethon and Gofannon among the anoethau, Trioedd Ynys Prydein (The Welsh Triads), ed. and trans. Rachel Bromwich, 3rd ed. (2006) — the Three Futile Battles; Cad Goddeu and Amathaon fab Dôn.
